verses.context: After the formal conclusion of 20:30-31 the story begins again: Jesus reveals himself once more to the disciples, this time in Galilee by the lake. The verse announces the theme of the first half of the chapter with a double statement of revelation, ‘he revealed himself... and he revealed himself in this way’.
verses.grammar: Meta tauta, ‘after these things’, is John's usual loose connective between episodes (5:1, 6:1, 7:1), so it does not by itself mark a new author. Ephanerōsen heauton palin, ‘he revealed himself again’, uses phaneroō, ‘to make manifest’, with the reflexive heauton: the risen Jesus shows himself when and to whom he chooses. The same verb framed the first sign, when Jesus revealed his glory at Cana (2:11). Ephanerōsen de houtōs, ‘and he revealed himself thus’, is a heading for the story that follows; houtōs, ‘in this way’, points forward. The lake is named thalassa tēs Tiberiados, ‘the sea of Tiberias’, as in 6:1.
verses.text: No surviving manuscript of John ends at 20:31; chapter 21 is in every copy that preserves the end of the Gospel. The question of its origin is literary. Rudolf Bultmann (1941), C. K. Barrett (1955), and Raymond Brown (1966 to 1970) judged it an epilogue added by the evangelist's circle, pointing to the apparent conclusion at 20:30-31, the ‘we’ of verse 24, and some vocabulary found only in this chapter (aigialos, ‘shore’; prosphagion, ‘fish’; ischuō, ‘be able’). Paul Minear (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1983) and Richard Bauckham (The Testimony of the Beloved Disciple, 2007) argued that it was planned from the start as the counterpart to the prologue, noting that much of the unusual vocabulary belongs to fishing, a subject the rest of the Gospel never treats. See 20:30-31 and 21:24.

verses.context: Seven disciples are together: Simon Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two others unnamed. The list gathers figures from the start and the end of the Gospel: Peter and Nathanael from the first calling (1:40-51), Thomas from the Easter scenes. The sons of Zebedee are named here for the only time in John.
verses.grammar: Ēsan homou, ‘they were together’, uses the same adverb as 20:4, where the two disciples ran together. Each name carries a note: Thōmas ho legomenos Didumos, ‘Thomas called the Twin’, as in 11:16 and 20:24; Nathanaēl ho apo Kana tēs Galilaias, ‘Nathanael from Cana of Galilee’, which is new information, since 1:45-49 did not name his town; hoi tou Zebedaiou, ‘those of Zebedee’, a genitive of relationship meaning his sons. Kai alloi ek tōn mathētōn autou duo, ‘and two others of his disciples’, leaves room for the beloved disciple, who appears in verse 7 without having been named in the list.
verses.history: Cana is usually identified with Khirbet Qana, a hill site about 14 kilometers north of Nazareth, where excavations have found remains of a Jewish village of the Roman period; the modern Christian pilgrimage town of Kafr Kanna, closer to Nazareth, is the traditional alternative. That the beloved disciple is one of ‘the sons of Zebedee’ or one of the two unnamed disciples cannot be decided from this verse, and the question has been argued both ways.

verses.context: Peter announces that he is going fishing, and the others go with him. They fish all night and catch nothing. The scene is ordinary work, and it sets up the sign that follows, as the empty nets of Luke 5:5 set up the call of the first disciples.
verses.grammar: Hupagō halieuein, ‘I am going to fish’, uses a present of immediate intention with an infinitive of purpose. Interpreters differ over whether it signals a return to the old life in discouragement or simply the need to earn a living while they wait; the grammar is neutral, and the Gospel passes no judgment. Erchometha kai hēmeis sun soi, ‘we too are coming with you’, uses the emphatic hēmeis. En ekeinē tē nukti epiasan ouden, ‘in that night they caught nothing’: piazō, ‘to seize’, is the verb John uses for the attempts to arrest Jesus (7:30, 7:44, 10:39, 11:57), and ouden, ‘nothing’, recalls 15:5, ‘apart from Me you can do nothing’.

verses.context: At daybreak Jesus stands on the shore, and the disciples do not recognize him. He calls out, ‘Children’, and asks whether they have anything to eat. They answer no. As with Mary in the garden (20:14), the risen Lord is present before he is known.
verses.grammar: Prōias de ēdē genomenēs, ‘when morning had already come’, is a genitive absolute; the Nestle-Aland and SBL editions print the aorist genomenēs, while Westcott and Hort printed the present ginomenēs, ‘as morning was coming on’, a difference of a few minutes of dawn. Estē Iēsous eis ton aigialon, ‘Jesus stood on the shore’, uses the same aorist estē as 20:19 and 20:26. Ou mentoi ēdeisan hoi mathētai hoti Iēsous estin, ‘the disciples, however, did not know that it was Jesus’, repeats almost exactly 20:14. Jesus' question, paidia, mē ti prosphagion echete; begins with mē, which expects the answer no: ‘Children, you haven't any fish, have you?’ Prosphagion is something eaten with bread, usually fish. Paidia, ‘children’, is a warm address used in 1 John 2:14 and 2:18.

verses.context: Jesus tells them to cast the net on the right side of the boat, promising that they will find fish. They obey, and the catch is so great that they cannot haul it in. The abundance matches the other signs of the Gospel, the wine at Cana and the bread by this same lake.
verses.grammar: Balete eis ta dexia merē tou ploiou to diktuon, ‘cast the net to the right side of the boat’, is an aorist imperative followed by the future heurēsete, ‘you will find’, a promise attached to a command. Diktuon is the general word for a fishing net. Ouketi auto helkusai ischuon, ‘they were no longer able to draw it’, uses helkō, ‘to draw’ or ‘drag’, the verb Jesus used when he said no one can come to him unless the Father draws him (6:44) and that, lifted up, he would draw all people to himself (12:32). Apo tou plēthous tōn ichthuōn, ‘because of the multitude of the fish’, uses apo for cause.
verses.history: Mendel Nun, a fisherman who studied the Sea of Galilee for decades, noted that shoals near the shore can sometimes be seen from land when those in a boat cannot see them, and that fishermen often relied on a watcher on shore. Such observations make the scene plausible without explaining it away; the Gospel presents the catch as a sign of the risen Lord's knowledge and provision.

theology.note: The verb for hauling the net is the Gospel's verb for Christ drawing people to himself (12:32). Many interpreters, from the fathers onward, have read the catch as a picture of the church's mission: fruitless without the Lord's word, abundant at his command.

verses.context: The beloved disciple is the first to recognize who is on the shore: “It is the Lord!” Peter, hearing it, wraps his outer garment around himself and throws himself into the sea. As at the tomb, one disciple sees first and the other acts first.
verses.grammar: Ho mathētēs ekeinos hon ēgapa ho Iēsous, ‘that disciple whom Jesus loved’, is the Gospel's fullest form of his title. His words, ho kurios estin, ‘it is the Lord’, echo Mary's ‘I have seen the Lord’ (20:18). Ton ependutēn diezōsato, ‘he girded on his outer garment’, uses ependutēs, a garment worn over another, perhaps a fisherman's smock, and diazōnnumi, ‘to tie around oneself’, the verb used when Jesus tied the towel around himself to wash the disciples' feet (13:4-5). Ēn gar gumnos, ‘for he was naked’, commonly means lightly clad, stripped for work. Ebalen heauton eis tēn thalassan, ‘he threw himself into the sea’, uses ballō, the verb of casting the net in verse 6.

theology.note: The disciple who knows himself loved is the first to recognize the Lord. The Gospel does not set this against Peter's eager love, which throws him into the sea; it shows two kinds of devotion, one that perceives and one that runs, both drawn to the same person.

verses.context: The other disciples come in the small boat, dragging the net full of fish, since they are only about a hundred yards from land. When they come ashore they see a charcoal fire with fish on it and bread. Jesus has already prepared a meal before any of their catch reaches him.
verses.grammar: Tō ploiariō, ‘in the little boat’, uses a diminutive of ploion, though the change may be stylistic, since verse 3 uses ploion for the same vessel. Hōs apo pēchōn diakosiōn, ‘about two hundred cubits away’, is roughly 90 meters. Surontes to diktuon, ‘dragging the net’, uses surō, ‘to drag’ or ‘haul’. In verse 9 blepousin, ‘they see’, is a historical present, and the objects are described with participles: anthrakian keimenēn, ‘a charcoal fire lying there’, kai opsarion epikeimenon, ‘and fish lying on it’, kai arton, ‘and bread’. Opsarion is singular and may be collective, ‘fish’, as in the feeding of the five thousand (6:9, 6:11); arton, ‘bread’, may also be collective.

theology.note: Before the disciples bring anything, the Lord has already made breakfast. The scene joins the miraculous catch to an ordinary meal cooked over coals: the one who provides abundance also provides daily bread, and he serves his servants.

verses.context: Jesus tells them to bring some of the fish they have just caught. Simon Peter goes aboard and hauls the net to land, full of large fish, a hundred and fifty-three, and the net is not torn. The count and the unbroken net are the two details John stops to record.
verses.grammar: Enegkate apo tōn opsariōn hōn epiasate nun, ‘bring some of the fish that you have now caught’, uses apo, ‘some of’, and hōn, a relative pronoun attracted into the genitive of its antecedent. Jesus invites them to add their catch to his meal. Anebē oun Simōn Petros, ‘so Simon Peter went up’, probably means he went aboard the boat or up onto the beach; eilkusen to diktuon eis tēn gēn, ‘he dragged the net to land’, uses helkō again (verse 6). The number is given in full, hekaton pentēkonta triōn, ‘a hundred fifty-three’. Kai tosoutōn ontōn ouk eschisthē to diktuon, ‘and though there were so many, the net was not torn’, uses a concessive genitive absolute and schizō, the verb of the untorn tunic (19:24) and the root of schisma, ‘division’ (7:43, 9:16, 10:19).
verses.history: The number has drawn many interpretations. Augustine noted that 153 is the sum of the numbers from 1 to 17 (a triangular number) and read 17 as the ten commandments joined to the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit, law with grace, so that the catch stands for all the saved (Tractates on John 122). Jerome, commenting on the fishermen of Ezekiel 47, said that the Greek writers on fish, above all the Cilician poet Oppian, counted 153 kinds, so the catch signified every kind of person; Oppian's surviving poem on fishing, the Halieutica, gives no such figure, and Robert Grant (Harvard Theological Review, 1949) found that Jerome's claim cannot be confirmed from it. Cyril of Alexandria divided the number into 100 (the fullness of the Gentiles), 50 (the remnant of Israel), and 3 (the Trinity). J. A. Emerton (Journal of Theological Studies, 1958) observed that in Ezekiel 47:10, where fishermen stand from En-gedi to En-eglaim beside the river flowing from the temple, the Hebrew letters of Gedi and Eglaim have numerical values of 17 and 153. Others take 153 simply as the remembered tally of fishermen who counted their catch.

theology.note: Whatever the number means, John stresses that the net held all the fish without tearing. The fathers read the unbroken net, like the untorn tunic, as a picture of the church's unity; the text itself shows the Lord's gathering as abundant and whole.

verses.context: Jesus invites them to breakfast. None of them dares to ask who he is, because they know it is the Lord. He takes the bread and gives it to them, and the fish likewise. The narrator counts this as the third time Jesus was revealed to the disciples after being raised from the dead.
verses.grammar: Deute aristēsate, ‘come, have breakfast’, joins the adverb deute, ‘come here’, to an aorist imperative of aristaō, ‘to eat the morning meal’. Oudeis de etolma tōn mathētōn exetasai auton, su tis ei; ‘none of the disciples dared to question him, Who are you?’, uses the imperfect etolma, ‘was daring’, and exetazō, ‘to inquire closely’. The next participle, eidotes hoti ho kurios estin, ‘knowing that it was the Lord’, creates a tension the Gospel leaves in place: they know him, and yet something about him silences the question. Verse 13 uses historical presents, erchetai... lambanei... didōsin, ‘he comes, takes, gives’, the same sequence as 6:11. In verse 14 egertheis ek nekrōn, ‘having been raised from the dead’, is an aorist passive: God raised him.

theology.note: The risen Jesus shares a meal with his disciples, as Peter later testifies: they ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead (Acts 10:41). The meal is part of the evidence that his rising was bodily, and it is also a sign of restored fellowship with those who had deserted him.

The actions of taking and giving bread and fish repeat the feeding of the five thousand (6:11), and many readers hear eucharistic overtones, as in Luke 24:30. John does not call it the Lord's Supper, and readers differ over how much sacramental meaning to find; the plain sense is a meal of fellowship given by the risen Lord.

verses.context: After breakfast Jesus turns to Peter and asks whether he loves him more than these. Peter answers yes, appealing to Jesus' own knowledge, and Jesus commissions him: feed my lambs. The first of three questions answers the first of three denials, and it is asked beside a charcoal fire, as the denials were.
verses.grammar: Jesus addresses him as Simōn Iōannou, ‘Simon son of John’, the name he used at their first meeting (1:42), not Peter. His question, agapas me pleon toutōn; ‘do you love me more than these?’, uses agapaō; pleon toutōn is ambiguous (more than these disciples love me, more than you love them, or more than these things). Peter answers nai, kurie, su oidas hoti philō se, ‘yes, Lord, you know that I love you’, with phileō. Whether the change of verb matters is one of the chapter's famous questions. B. F. Westcott read agapaō as the higher love of will and esteem and Peter as claiming only affection; R. C. Trench (Synonyms of the New Testament) held phileō the warmer word. Against any distinction, Augustine observed that the questions use two verbs for one love (City of God 14.7), and many modern commentators, among them C. K. Barrett, Raymond Brown, and D. A. Carson, note that John uses both verbs for the Father's love of the Son (3:35, 5:20), for Jesus' love of Lazarus (11:3, 11:5), and for the beloved disciple (13:23, 20:2), that the Septuagint uses both in Genesis 37:3-4 and in one sentence in Proverbs 8:17, and that the passage varies its other words too.

theology.note: Jesus asks Peter about love, not courage or competence. The one who had boasted of greater loyalty than the others (Mark 14:29) now claims only what Jesus himself knows. Love for Christ is the root of the commission, and it is shown in feeding those who belong to him.

Restoration begins with Peter's old name and a question that recalls his boast. Jesus neither ignores the denial nor rehearses it; he brings Peter to confess love in dependence on the Lord's knowledge, which is the shape of true repentance.

verses.context: Jesus asks a second time, now without ‘more than these’, and Peter gives the same answer. The commission changes from feeding lambs to shepherding sheep: care for the flock includes guidance and protection as well as nourishment.
verses.grammar: Legei autō palin deuteron, ‘he says to him again, a second time’, doubles the adverbs for emphasis. The question is simpler: Simōn Iōannou, agapas me; ‘Simon son of John, do you love me?’, still with agapaō. Peter's answer repeats the first word for word. The command changes both verb and object: poimaine ta probata mou, ‘shepherd my sheep’. Poimainō, ‘to shepherd’, is broader than boskō, ‘to feed’, and includes leading and protecting; probata, ‘sheep’, replaces arnia, ‘lambs’. The possessive mou, ‘my’, never changes: the flock is Christ's, not Peter's.

theology.note: The risen Shepherd entrusts his own sheep to an under-shepherd. The church's leaders shepherd a flock that belongs to Christ and answer to him for it, which is how Paul charges the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:28) and how 1 Peter 5:1-4 charges elders under the chief Shepherd. Churches differ on how far this charge was unique to Peter.

ot.note: Ezekiel condemns Israel's shepherds for feeding themselves instead of the flock and promises that the LORD will set over his sheep one shepherd, his servant David, who will feed them. The Septuagint uses poimanei and poimēn, the same word family as Jesus' command. Jesus, the good shepherd of chapter 10, fulfills the promise and then appoints Peter as a shepherd under him, so the charge carries Ezekiel's warning: to feed the sheep, not to feed on them.

verses.context: The third time Jesus asks, now using Peter's own verb, and Peter is grieved because he has been asked a third time. He answers by appealing to Jesus' complete knowledge: ‘Lord, You know all things’. Jesus gives the third commission, and the three denials have been answered by three confessions.
verses.grammar: Legei autō to triton, ‘he says to him the third time’. The question now uses phileō: phileis me; ‘do you love me?’ Elupēthē ho Petros hoti eipen autō to triton, ‘Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time’: the reason given is the repetition, not the change of verb, which is why many interpreters doubt the distinction matters. Peter's answer uses two verbs of knowing, kurie, panta su oidas, su ginōskeis hoti philō se, ‘Lord, you know all things, you know that I love you’; oida and ginōskō are also largely interchangeable in John, and the pairing strengthens the appeal. John has said that Jesus knew what was in every person (2:24-25), and the disciples confessed that he knew all things (16:30). The final command is boske ta probata mou, ‘feed my sheep’.

theology.note: Peter's grief is the pain of remembered failure brought into the open, and it leads not to despair but to confession. He no longer relies on his own promise but on the Lord's knowledge of his heart, and he is recommissioned in that dependence.

The one who failed most publicly is given the care of the flock. Leadership in Christ's church rests on grace received, not on a record without failure; Peter's later exhortation to humble shepherding (1 Peter 5:2-5) comes from a man who knew this morning.

verses.context: With a solemn ‘truly, truly’ Jesus tells Peter what his following will cost. When young he dressed himself and went where he wished; when old he will stretch out his hands, and another will dress him and take him where he does not want to go. The narrator explains that this signified the death by which Peter would glorify God, and Jesus says to him, “Follow Me.”
verses.grammar: Amēn amēn legō soi, ‘truly, truly I say to you’, is the solemn formula Jesus uses throughout John, last spoken to Peter when he foretold the denial (13:38). Two sentences contrast youth and age: hote ēs neōteros, ezōnnues seauton kai periepateis hopou ētheles, ‘when you were younger, you used to dress yourself and walk where you wanted’, with three imperfects of habit; and hotan gērasēs, ekteneis tas cheiras sou, kai allos se zōsei kai oisei hopou ou theleis, ‘when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish’. Stretching out the hands was used by ancient writers for crucifixion; Justin Martyr applies Isaiah 65:2, ‘I have spread out My hands’, to the cross (First Apology 35). Verse 19 repeats the formula sēmainōn poiō thanatō, ‘signifying by what kind of death’, used of Jesus in 12:33 and 18:32, and akolouthei moi is a present imperative: ‘keep following me’.
verses.history: Early Christian writers understood the saying as fulfilled in Peter's death in Rome under Nero. Tertullian wrote that at Rome Peter endured a passion like his Lord's (Prescription against Heretics 36) and read the girding as the binding of Peter to the cross (Scorpiace 15); Eusebius reports, citing Origen, that Peter asked to be crucified head downward (Church History 3.1). The earliest reference to Peter's martyrdom, in 1 Clement 5, written from Rome about AD 96, does not describe the manner of his death.

theology.note: Jesus tells Peter plainly that following him will lead to a death not of his choosing. The call to follow is not withdrawn because it is costly; it is given with the cost in view, as Jesus warned that a servant is not greater than his master (15:20).

Peter's death will glorify God, the same language John uses for Jesus' own death (12:23, 13:31, 17:1). The martyr's death is joined to the Lord's, and what looks like defeat becomes a display of God's glory.

verses.context: Peter turns and sees the beloved disciple following them, the one who had leaned back on Jesus' chest at the supper and asked who would betray him. Peter asks what will happen to him. Having just heard his own future, Peter wants to know another's.
verses.grammar: Epistrapheis ho Petros blepei, ‘Peter, having turned, sees’, combines an aorist passive participle used with middle sense (‘turning himself’) and a historical present. Ton mathētēn hon ēgapa ho Iēsous akolouthounta, ‘the disciple whom Jesus loved, following’, uses akoloutheō in its plain sense, walking behind, just after Jesus has said ‘Follow me’ to Peter; the beloved disciple is already doing what Peter has been told to do. The relative clause recalls 13:23-25 with anepesen en tō deipnō epi to stēthos autou, ‘he leaned back at the supper on his chest’, and tis estin ho paradidous se; ‘who is the one betraying you?’ Peter's question, kurie, houtos de ti; is elliptical, literally ‘Lord, and this one, what?’

verses.context: Jesus refuses to answer Peter's curiosity: if he wills that the other disciple remain until he comes, that is not Peter's concern; Peter must follow. The narrator then corrects a rumor that spread among the believers, that this disciple would not die. Jesus did not say that; he said only, ‘If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?’
verses.grammar: Ean auton thelō menein heōs erchomai, ‘if I want him to remain until I come’, uses ean with a present subjunctive, a hypothetical condition that asserts nothing about what Jesus actually wills. Heōs erchomai, ‘until I come’, uses a present indicative with heōs, a common idiom for a future event. Ti pros se; ‘what is that to you?’, is a brusque idiom. Su moi akolouthei, ‘you, follow me’, puts su first for emphasis: each disciple has his own calling. In verse 23 exēlthen houtos ho logos eis tous adelphous, ‘this word went out among the brothers’, uses adelphoi for the community of believers, following Jesus' ‘my brothers’ in 20:17. The narrator quotes Jesus' words exactly to show that the rumor misread a conditional as a promise.
verses.history: The correction suggests that the beloved disciple lived to a great age, long enough for believers to think Jesus would return first, and many interpreters, among them Rudolf Bultmann and Raymond Brown, take it as evidence that he had died by the time the chapter was written and that his death had unsettled the community. Others think he was still living but very old. Irenaeus says John lived at Ephesus into the reign of Trajan, who became emperor in AD 98 (Against Heresies 3.3.4). Augustine reports, without accepting it, a story that John lay asleep in his tomb at Ephesus with the earth stirring above him (Tractates on John 124).

theology.note: Jesus speaks of his coming as certain, ‘until I come’, while refusing to attach it to any person's lifespan or any date. The narrator's correction warns against building expectations about the time of the return on words that do not say what we wish.
Peter will follow to martyrdom; the other disciple may remain. The Lord assigns each his own path, and the proper response to another's calling is not comparison but obedience: ‘you, follow me’.

verses.context: The Gospel names its witness: the disciple of the preceding verses is the one who testifies to these things and has written them. Then a ‘we’ adds its own confirmation: we know that his testimony is true. The whole book rests, by its own account, on the testimony of an eyewitness.
verses.grammar: Houtos estin ho mathētēs ho marturōn peri toutōn kai ho grapsas tauta, ‘this is the disciple who is testifying about these things and who wrote these things’. The present participle marturōn presents his witness as ongoing, and the aorist grapsas as completed. Graphō can mean ‘to cause to be written’, as when Pilate ‘wrote’ the title (19:19, 19:22), so the phrase need not exclude a secretary or helper. Kai oidamen hoti alēthēs autou hē marturia estin, ‘and we know that his testimony is true’, is the verse's central puzzle. On one reading the ‘we’ is a group, the evangelist's community or its leaders, vouching for the disciple after his death (Raymond Brown, C. K. Barrett). Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) argued that it is the ‘we’ of authoritative testimony, the author speaking of himself with the weight of a witness, as in 1:14, 3:11, 1 John 1:1-5, and 3 John 12, where the elder writes “you know that our testimony is true.”

theology.note: The Gospel grounds itself not in inspiration detached from history but in the testimony of someone who saw, and it asks to be received as true testimony (19:35). Christian faith rests on apostolic witness written down, which is why the church has always valued the eyewitness roots of its Scriptures.

verses.context: The Gospel ends by confessing its own limits. Jesus did many other things, and if every one were written down, the narrator supposes, the world itself could not hold the books. The last word of the book turns from what is written to the one who cannot be contained by writing.
verses.grammar: Estin de kai alla polla ha epoiēsen ho Iēsous, ‘there are also many other things that Jesus did’, echoes 20:30. Hatina ean graphētai kath' hen, ‘which, if they were written one by one’, uses ean with a present subjunctive and the distributive kath' hen, ‘each one’. Oud' auton oimai ton kosmon chōrēsai ta graphomena biblia, ‘not even the world itself, I suppose, would contain the books being written’, is the only place in the Gospel where the narrator speaks in the first person singular, with oimai, ‘I think’ or ‘I suppose’. Chōreō means ‘to have room for’. The statement is deliberate hyperbole, a figure ancient readers recognized as praise.
verses.history: Ancient histories often closed by noting that much remained untold. The Old Testament books of Kings end reigns by referring readers to records not included (1 Kings 11:41), and 1 Maccabees 9:22 says that the rest of the deeds of Judas Maccabeus were not written because they were very many. John's closing hyperbole belongs to this convention and heightens it: the subject is not a king or a general but the one through whom the world was made (1:3, 1:10).
verses.text: The manuscripts divide between the aorist infinitive chōrēsai, printed in the Nestle-Aland text, and the future infinitive chōrēsein, printed by Westcott and Hort and the SBL edition; the meaning is the same. The King James Version adds ‘Amen’ at the end, following later manuscripts; the earliest witnesses lack it.

theology.note: The Gospel is selective by design (20:30-31), and it says so without apology. What is written is enough for faith and life; it is not the whole of Christ. The closing confession keeps the reader from mistaking the book for its subject.
